source: Edward Alexander Samuells, Notes on a Forest Race Called Puttooas or Juanga, Inhabiting Certain of the Tributary Mehals of Cuttack, Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal 25(4), printed pp. 295–303
edition_date: The original article and running heads print 1856; the Biodiversity Heritage Library catalog lists the volume's article as 1857. Citation follows the printed 1856 date and records this catalog discrepancy.
scope: Entire printed Juang vocabulary on pp. 302–303 only, corresponding to PDF pages 334–335 of the 790-page scan; 31 printed prompt cells. Article prose and ethnographic images are outside lexical scope.
alternates: The source prints Da or Dagé under water. Both alternatives are included with distinct variant-qualified entry keys and the same prompt locator.
holds: Eleven prompts are held: woman, child, food, ten men, horse, we are, you are, I am, to give, to come, to go. Most are multiword or inflected phrases. The single printed horse token Ghorardendite may be an unanalysed compound or inflected response and is held conservatively.
rights: The Biodiversity Heritage Library marks its digitized volume 25 as public domain; the underlying article was printed in 1856. The whole scan and rendered images remain local review cache and are not installed. The source package contains only attributed lexical forms, glosses, and factual provenance/locators, not article prose or page images.
provenance: Samuells states on printed p. 301 that he collected the words and phrases himself. He first met Puttooas/Juang in Dhekenal in 1854, saw another group in Hindole in 1855, and visited a village near Bhapore weeks before writing in 1856. He does not assign individual glossary items to those visits or to speakers, so the source-qualified Juang lect has blank coordinates and only this broad historical locality note.
comparison_source: Dalton 1866, Appendix F pp. 266–267, has a Putoons/Juang column, but its underlying collector is unclear. Dalton cites Samuells 1856 for ethnography; the two printed vocabularies are materially nonidentical (for example, Samuells man Moolusso vs. Dalton juang, woman Khemé chélo or Juangurrakeo vs. Dalton mukha). Dalton remains analysis-only and is not used as a second independent witness here. The Dalton public-domain scan is https://www.loc.gov/item/tmp92008019/ (local cache SHA-256 17a81c5ad648497061aa6067abe9e1eb866df30934af225e8f13ae52e2178717).
transcription: All 31 glossary cells were visually checked against the printed pages, including 11 held items. Original romanized capitalization and acute accents are preserved in Original; the Form field case-folds it. Rice is printed Runkoo, not OCR Kunkoo. No phonetic interpretation is claimed for source doubling or acute accents beyond the conservative source profile; the original spelling remains primary.
overlap: Screened 2,028 existing Juang source rows. Only one normalized exact-form match among the 21 selected forms: Samuells Minna 'one' and later Pinnow 1959 minna 'one, one single'. Pinnow's underlying Juang source for this item is not resolved; retain both source-qualified citations and do not claim they are independent elicitations. No Samuells record is already installed.
audit: reviewed_inventory.tsv accounts for every printed glossary prompt. audit.jsonl and source CSV are generated from that inventory. visual-review-20260925.jsonl records 31 print checks; overlap-review.json records the one normalized match.
inapplicable: No native script, dictionary sense numbering, etymological labels, donor claims, reference IDs, or source cognacy assertions are printed in this two-page glossary. No etymology or graph edges are inferred.
deferred: The user expressly prohibited database builds and remote execution. Full build, graph/reference validation and browser QA are deferred; this is a bounded source-stage glossary, not an ingestion of article prose or other Juang sources.
